summary: This document describes how to obtain IPv4 configuration dynamically in IPv6 networks by carrying DHCPv4 messages over DHCPv6 transport. It defines two new DHCPv6 messages and two new DHCPv6 options, so users on IPv6-only uplinks can still get IPv4 settings.

plainLanguage.summary: DHCPv4 asks for an address by broadcasting over IPv4, so it cannot work on a link that carries IPv6 only. This RFC carries the DHCPv4 messages inside DHCPv6 messages instead, so they travel over the IPv6 network to a server that understands them. The client sees an ordinary DHCPv4 exchange, and the server sees an ordinary DHCPv4 message, so the existing infrastructure carries on working unchanged.

subtitle: How a device on an IPv6-only uplink gets its IPv4 settings by carrying DHCPv4 messages inside DHCPv6.

tldr.problem: As networks move to IPv6, some links will carry IPv6 only, but devices on them may still need IPv4 configuration, including addresses of IPv4-only services. The DHCPv4 protocol cannot cross such a link, because it depends on IPv4 broadcast.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two new DHCPv6 messages, DHCPv4-query and DHCPv4-response, and two new options. A DHCPv4 message is put inside a DHCPv4 Message option and carried in the payload of the DHCPv6 message, over the IPv6 network, reaching an ordinary DHCPv4 server.
tldr.outcome: The existing DHCPv4 infrastructure is reused, including failover, DNS updates and lease queries, and a client on an IPv6-only link can still obtain IPv4 configuration. The mechanism is optional and is meant for specific transition environments rather than general use.

today: RFC 7341 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2014, and the unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it. IANA has allocated the message types 20 and 21 and the option codes 87 and 88 for its use.

sections.title: Why Carry DHCPv4 Inside DHCPv6
sections.content:
As the migration towards IPv6 continues, IPv6-only networks become more prevalent. In such networks, IPv4 connectivity continues to be provided as a service over IPv6-only networks. In addition to provisioning IPv4 addresses for clients of this service, other IPv4 configuration parameters may also be needed, for example the addresses of IPv4-only services.

The RFC describes a transport mechanism to carry DHCPv4 messages using the DHCPv6 protocol, for the dynamic provisioning of IPv4 addresses and other DHCPv4 specific configuration parameters across IPv6-only networks. It leverages the existing DHCPv4 infrastructure, such as failover, DNS updates and DHCP Leasequery.

When IPv6 multicast is used to transport the messages, there is a further benefit: the operator can gain information about the underlying IPv6 network to which the client is connected from the DHCPv6 relay agents through which the request has passed.

The document defines the terms it uses. Customer Premises Equipment (CPE) provides access for devices on a local area network, typically at the customer's site or home, to the service provider's network. The DHCP 4o6 client is a DHCP client that supports both DHCPv6 and the DHCPv4 over DHCPv6 protocol, and can therefore request IPv6 configuration with DHCPv6 and IPv4 configuration with DHCPv4 over DHCPv6. The DHCP 4o6 server is a DHCP server able to process DHCPv4 packets encapsulated in the DHCPv4 Message option.
sections.plainLanguage:
DHCPv4 gets an address for a device by sending a broadcast over IPv4. On a link that carries IPv6 only, that broadcast has nowhere to go, so the device cannot ask for an IPv4 address at all.

This RFC puts the whole DHCPv4 exchange inside DHCPv6 messages. The device still speaks ordinary DHCPv4 to the server, and the server still behaves as an ordinary DHCPv4 server. Nothing on either side has to change except the transport between them.

sections.title: The Deployment and the Message Flow
sections.content:
The architecture addresses a typical use case, where a DHCP client's uplink supports IPv6 only and the service provider's network supports IPv6 and limited IPv4 services. The client can only use the IPv6 network to reach IPv4 services, so IPv4 services must be configured using IPv6 as the underlying network protocol.

Although the purpose of the document is to address the communication between the DHCPv4 client and the DHCPv4 server, the mechanism does not restrict the transported message types to DHCPv4 only. Because the DHCPv4 message is a special type of BOOTP message, BOOTP messages (RFC 951) may also be transported using the same mechanism.

DHCP clients may be running on customer premises equipment, on end hosts, or on any other device that supports the DHCP client function; the document uses the CPE as an example, without precluding any end host from implementing this in future.

The mechanism works by carrying DHCPv4 messages encapsulated within the newly defined DHCPv6 messages. The client implements a new DHCPv6 message called DHCPv4-query, which carries a DHCPv4 message in the new DHCPv4 Message option, and it may be transmitted either through DHCPv6 relay agents or directly to the server. The server replies with a new DHCPv6 message called DHCPv4-response, which carries the DHCPv4 message from the server in the same option.

Before the client can use DHCPv4 over DHCPv6, it MUST obtain the necessary IPv6 configuration. It requests the DHCP 4o6 Server Address option by sending the option code in an Option Request option. If the server responds with that option, it is an indication to the client to attempt using DHCPv4 over DHCPv6 to obtain IPv4 configuration; otherwise the client MUST NOT use DHCPv4 over DHCPv6. The client obtains the addresses of the servers from the option and uses them to communicate with them. If the option contains no addresses, the client uses the well-known All_DHCP_Relay_Agents_and_Servers multicast address.

Before applying for an IPv4 address through a DHCPv4-query message, the client must identify a suitable network interface for the address. Once the request is acknowledged by the server, the client can configure the address and the other relevant parameters on that interface. The mechanism for determining a suitable interface is out of the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage:
The usual case is a device whose uplink carries IPv6 only, in a provider network that also offers some IPv4 services. The device can reach those IPv4 services only by way of the IPv6 network, so its IPv4 settings have to be configured over IPv6.

The flow has two parts. First the device asks its normal DHCPv6 server, in the ordinary way, whether IPv4-over-DHCPv6 is available here; the server answers with an option listing the addresses of the servers that can serve IPv4 requests. Then the device sends its DHCPv4 request inside a DHCPv6 message, and the answer comes back the same way.

Nothing in the DHCPv6 relay path is changed in a way that affects IPv6. The relay encapsulation is used solely to deliver the DHCPv4 packets to a DHCPv4-capable server.

sections.title: The Two New DHCPv6 Messages
sections.content:
Two new DHCPv6 messages carry the DHCPv4 messages between the client and the server. DHCPV4-QUERY has message type 20 and is sent by the client to the server; the DHCPv4 Message option it carries holds the DHCPv4 message the client uses to request IPv4 configuration parameters. DHCPV4-RESPONSE has message type 21 and is sent by the server to the client; it contains a DHCPv4 Message option carrying the DHCPv4 message the server produced in response to the one it received.

Both messages share the same format: a message type field, a flags field, and a variable-length options field. The message type identifies the message as either DHCPv4-query or DHCPv4-response. The flags field carries additional information needed by the server to process the encapsulated DHCPv4 message in a query, or by the client to process the encapsulated DHCPv4 message in a response. The options field MUST carry the DHCPv4 Message option, and only DHCPv6 options for IPv4 configuration may be included in it; it MUST NOT contain DHCPv6 options related solely to IPv6 or to IPv6-only service configuration.

The flags field of the DHCPv4-query carries only one bit in use, with the rest reserved. The U bit is the Unicast flag: when set to 1 it indicates that the DHCPv4 message inside would have been sent to a unicast address if it had been sent using IPv4, and when set to 0 that it would have been sent to the broadcast address. The remaining bits MUST be set to zero when sending and MUST be ignored when receiving. The DHCPv4-response has no flags defined; the server MUST set all bits of that field to zero and the client MUST ignore the contents of the field.
sections.plainLanguage:
The two new messages look like any other DHCPv6 message: a type number, a flags field, and a list of options. The type numbers are 20 for the query and 21 for the response, both in the space reserved for DHCPv6 message types.

The flags field of the query carries one bit, and it exists to solve a problem caused by the change of transport. A DHCPv4 client normally sends some messages to a single server and others to everyone, and the server can tell the difference by the IPv4 address it received the message on. Over IPv6 that address says nothing about the inner message, so the client has to say it explicitly in this bit.

sections.title: The Two New DHCPv6 Options
sections.content:
The DHCPv4 Message option carries a DHCPv4 message sent by the client or the server. Such messages exclude any IP or UDP headers. The option has the usual option-code and option-len fields, followed by the DHCPv4 message itself. The option code is OPTION_DHCPV4_MSG, 87, and the option-len is the length of the DHCPv4 message. In a DHCPv4-query message the option holds the message sent by the client; in a DHCPv4-response message it holds the message the server sent in reply.

The DHCP 4o6 Server Address option is sent by a server to a client that is requesting IPv6 configuration with DHCPv6. It carries a list of the IPv6 addresses of the DHCP 4o6 servers that the client should contact to obtain IPv4 configuration. The list may include multicast and unicast addresses, and the client sends its requests to all the unique addresses carried in it. The option may also carry no IPv6 addresses at all, which instructs the client to use the All_DHCP_Relay_Agents_and_Servers multicast address as the destination.

The presence of this option in the server's response indicates to the client that it should use DHCPv4 over DHCPv6. If the option is absent, the client MUST NOT enable the DHCPv4-over-DHCPv6 functionality. The option code is OPTION_DHCP4_O_DHCP6_SERVER, 88, the option-len is the length of the IPv6 addresses carried by the option, that is a multiple of 16 octets, and the minimal length is 0.
sections.plainLanguage:
Two options do the work. One is the envelope: the DHCPv4 message itself, without its IP and UDP headers, is placed inside a DHCPv6 option and carried in the payload of the DHCPv6 message. The other tells the client where to send those requests, as a list of server addresses.

The address list may be empty, and then the client is to use the standard multicast address for DHCP servers. The option's length is always a multiple of 16, because each address is 16 bytes long.

sections.title: What the Client and Server Do
sections.content:
The client MUST obtain the necessary IPv6 configuration from a DHCPv6 server before using DHCPv4 over DHCPv6. It requests the DHCP 4o6 Server Address option using the Option Request option in every Solicit, Request, Renew, Rebind and Information-request message. If the server includes the option in its response, the client can use DHCPv4 over DHCPv6. If it does not, the client MUST NOT use it to request IPv4 configuration. If the IPv6 configuration that contained the option later expires, or the renewed IPv6 configuration does not contain it, the client MUST stop using DHCPv4 over DHCPv6 to request or renew IPv4 configuration, though it continues to request the option for as long as it wants to use the mechanism.

In a multihomed configuration there may be more than one DHCPv6 configuration containing the option active at the same time. The configurations are then treated as independent, so that when any of them is active the function may be enabled for that configuration. An implementation may instead treat them as exclusive, keeping one configuration active continuously while it is valid and activating another when it becomes invalid. Which strategy to follow depends on the implementation: keeping several active may give useful redundancy in some applications and be needlessly complex in others.

If the client receives the option and DHCPv4 is in use on the interface over which the DHCPv6 option was received, the client MUST stop using the IPv4 configuration received that way, MAY send a DHCPRELEASE to relinquish the existing lease, and MUST NOT use DHCPv4 on that interface for as long as it keeps receiving the option.

If the option contains no addresses, the client MUST send its requests to the All_DHCP_Relay_Agents_and_Servers multicast address; if it carries a list, the client SHOULD send requests to each unique address. A client that obtained stateless IPv6 configuration with an Information-request message MUST follow the rules of RFC 4242 to refresh the DHCPv4-over-DHCPv6 configuration periodically, and a client with stateful IPv6 configuration refreshes the status of the function when it extends the lifetime of its IPv6 address with Renew and Rebind messages.

The client MUST use an IPv6 address of an appropriate scope as the source of the DHCPv4-query message: a link-local address when sending to the multicast address, and an address of appropriate scope acquired in advance when sending by unicast. It generates the DHCPv4 message and stores it verbatim in the DHCPv4 Message option, MUST put exactly one such option in a single DHCPv4-query message, and MUST NOT request the DHCP 4o6 Server Address option in the query. On receiving a DHCPv4-response it MUST look for the DHCPv4 Message option, discard the response if it is not there, and otherwise extract the DHCPv4 message and process it as described in Section 4.4 of RFC 2131. It follows the normal DHCPv4 retransmission requirements, implements RFC 4361 so that the device identifies itself correctly, and MUST send a client identifier option.

When the server receives a DHCPv4-query it searches for the DHCPv4 Message option and discards a packet without it. If it finds a valid option it extracts the original DHCPv4 message. Because that message is encapsulated in a DHCPv6 message, it lacks the information a DHCPv4 server normally uses to make address allocation decisions, such as giaddr for relayed messages and the IPv4 address of the interface used to reach a directly connected client. The DHCP 4o6 server therefore allocates addresses according to its own local address assignment policies: for a relayed request it MAY use the link-address field of the Relay-forward message to look up the IPv4 subnet, and for a directly connected client it MAY use the IPv6 source address of the message to determine the IPv4 subnet.

When it has created the response, the server places the DHCPv4 message in the payload of a DHCPv4 Message option and puts that into the DHCPv4-response message. If the query was received directly, the response MUST be unicast from the interface on which the original message was received. If the query arrived in a Relay-forward message, the server creates a Relay-reply message with the DHCPv4-response in the payload of a Relay Message option and responds as described in Section 20.3 of RFC 3315.
sections.plainLanguage:
The client asks for the server address option in every DHCPv6 message it sends, and uses it only while the server keeps giving it. With several connections, the implementation chooses whether to keep several such configurations alive at once.

One rule protects the network. If ordinary DHCPv4 is running on the same interface, the client must stop using it, because otherwise two servers could hand out addresses for the same link.

The server has one problem to solve. A DHCPv4 message normally carries the address of the interface it arrived on, which is how the server picks the subnet to allocate from. Wrapped in DHCPv6 that information is gone, so the server falls back on its own policy, using the relay's link address or the IPv6 source address of the request.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
DHCPv4 messages are encapsulated in the newly defined option and messages, which is similar to the handling of the current relay agent messages. In order to bypass firewalls or network authentication gateways, a malicious attacker may leverage this feature to convey other messages using DHCPv6, that is, use DHCPv6 as a form of encapsulation. The potential risk from this is no more severe than that with the current DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 practice.

It is possible for a rogue server to reply with a DHCP 4o6 Server Address option containing duplicated IPv6 addresses, which could cause an amplification attack. To avoid this, the client MUST check whether there are duplicate IPv6 addresses in the option when receiving one, and MUST ignore any but the first instance of each address.

One important consideration in deciding whether to enable DHCPv4 over DHCPv6 is that enabling it gives the DHCPv6 server the ability to shut off DHCPv4 traffic, and consequently IPv4 traffic, on the interface configured to do DHCPv4 over DHCPv6. For this reason it should only be enabled where there is a clear trust relationship that removes the concern. The RFC gives the example of a customer premises device enabling it on its WAN interface, because it is reasonable to assume that an internet service provider will not accidentally configure the service on that link, and that it would be impractical for an attacker to set up a rogue DHCPv6 server in the provider's network.
sections.plainLanguage:
Wrapping one protocol inside another gives an attacker a new tunnel to try, so the document says the risk is no worse than the existing practice with DHCPv4 and DHCPv6.

One attack is worth naming. A rogue server could send an address list with the same address repeated many times, and the client would send its request to each one, multiplying the traffic. The client therefore has to ignore repeated addresses.

The last point is a design warning rather than a rule. Once the mechanism is on, the DHCPv6 server can switch IPv4 off on that interface, so it should only be enabled where the operator trusts the server it is talking to.

messages.note: Carries the addresses of the servers that serve IPv4 requests.

messages.note: The DHCPv4 request inside a DHCPv4 Message option.

messages.label: DHCPv4-query
messages.note: Relayed to the configured DHCP 4o6 server address.

messages.label: DHCPv4-response
messages.note: The DHCPv4 answer inside a DHCPv4 Message option.

messages.label: DHCPv4-response
messages.note: The client extracts the DHCPv4 message and processes it as usual.
